key_finding: A nudge that shrouds the minimum-payment autopay default cut exact-minimum-payment behavior by 23% over six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, because liquidity-constrained cardholders simply chose autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum.
methodology: Field experiment on credit cards, six-month follow-up, National Bureau of Economic Research working paper.
why_it_matters: Directly supports the support team's worry: a choice-architecture change can shift nominal enrollment/behavior sharply while leaving the real outcome (debt/savings) unchanged, which is exactly the enrollment-vs-amount distinction the brief asks us to test before defaulting everyone into round-ups.
limitations: credit card debt paydown, not savings accumulation
shrouding a payment option differs structurally from opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrollment
relevance_reason: Consumer financial field experiment showing a default/nudge changes surface behavior without changing the underlying financial outcome, the core 'vanity metric' concern in the brief.

key_finding: A 2024 overview synthesizes plan-design evidence on automatic enrollment, default investment options, and framing, noting both participation gains and potential negative effects on participant engagement.
methodology: Narrative overview of defined-contribution plan design literature. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a single up-to-date synthesis of the engagement-versus-participation trade-off in the largest analogous literature, useful as a background map even though the mechanism (employer intermediary) does not transfer.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer self-directed product
narrative synthesis, not a systematic review with pooled effect sizes
relevance_reason: Broad, recent synthesis of the default/engagement trade-off in the closest analogous literature named by the brief.

key_finding: Default enrollment raises retirement plan participation in the short term but induces 'passivity' -- low contribution rates, non-management, and account churn -- that undermines simple participation-rate metrics as a welfare measure.
methodology: Policy discussion/narrative review of default enrollment literature. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: States plainly, in policy-essay form, the exact critique the support team is making about vanity enrollment metrics, and proposes mitigations (auto-escalation, re-enrollment reminders) that could translate into round-up feature design tweaks.
limitations: employer retirement plan setting, not consumer app
essay-style argument rather than new empirical estimates
no citation count/impact yet
relevance_reason: Directly frames the passivity-vs-participation tension the brief asks about, even though set in retirement plans.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework for when default effects persist, fade, or reverse downstream, driven by the time course of choice/consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and salience of trade-offs.
methodology: Theoretical synthesis and taxonomy-building across the consumer-default literature. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete list of moderators (antecedent preferences, trade-off salience, time course) the team should measure when evaluating whether round-up enrollment defaults persist past sign-up -- directly shapes what the 6-12 month follow-up study should track.
limitations: conceptual framework, not a new empirical estimate
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: General-purpose consumer psychology framework for exactly the downstream persistence/disengagement question the brief raises.

key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive to the value of the default option, even when it causes substantial losses.
methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default options in a large administrative claims setting.
why_it_matters: Strong causal evidence that default persistence can reflect true inattention rather than considered choice -- a caution against assuming opt-out enrollment reflects genuine preference, relevant to the manipulation-risk question.
limitations: government health-insurance enrollment, not a consumer fintech product
no employer-style trusted intermediary but also no app/liquidity context
relevance_reason: Rigorous natural-experiment evidence on default persistence and insensitivity to value, informing how much weight to put on opt-out enrollment numbers.

key_finding: Accounting for job turnover, vesting, and opt-outs, automatic enrollment raises steady-state savings by only 0.6% of income and auto-escalation by 0.3%, with only 40% of employees escalating on their first scheduled date.
methodology: Analysis of administrative data from nine 401(k) plans incorporating medium- and long-run dynamics (turnover, withdrawal, opt-out).
why_it_matters: The clearest quantitative statement of the support team's objection: once you follow people past enrollment, automatic-default effects on real savings amounts are much smaller than the headline enrollment-rate lift suggests.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans, not liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated auto-escalation differs from a self-set multiplier
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the 'defaults always help' premise with quantified medium/long-run attenuation, exactly the evidence the brief asked us to find.

key_finding: Germany's nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees raised pension participation by 23 percentage points, but most enrollees actively opted back out, and the default effect was strongest when incentives were high and knowledge of enrollment status was low.
methodology: Natural experiment using nationwide policy rollout, linked administrative and survey data.
why_it_matters: Shows a large default effect size decaying quickly through active opt-out, and ties the effect's strength to complexity/incentive salience and awareness -- relevant to whether our round-up default would similarly erode once users notice they're enrolled.
limitations: public pay-as-you-go pension system, not a consumer app
low-income employee population may not generalize
relevance_reason: Large, credible effect-size estimate on default enrollment with explicit heterogeneity by incentive/complexity, close to the brief's C1/C5 questions.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's gains on participation and contributions, replicated at 12 months, are substantially attenuated by 36 months, though the policy still meaningfully reduces savings inequality; a life-cycle model fits the pattern with a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Panel analysis of over 100 US retirement plans plus a UK representative panel, combined with a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete medium-run (36-month) attenuation estimate for default effects and quantifies the switching cost driving inertia -- directly useful for setting expectations about how much a round-up default will fade by 6-12 months.
limitations: US/UK retirement plans, not a liquid consumer savings product
structural model estimates, not directly observed switching costs
relevance_reason: Best available medium-run persistence estimate for default enrollment effects, even though set in retirement plans.

key_finding: Across three experiments including a representative five-country European sample (n=4207), default nudges produced medium-to-large effects on risk-taking, but implementing a default -- especially one the client then refuses -- significantly lowered how trustworthy and honest the advice was perceived to be.
methodology: Three behavioral experiments, including a large representative multi-country European experiment, on financial default framing in wealth management.
why_it_matters: Empirically shows the exact reputational trade-off the brief flags: a default that moves behavior can simultaneously read as manipulative and damage perceived trust, which should directly weigh against opt-out and toward active-choice or careful framing for entry design.
limitations: wealth-management advice context, not a mobile round-up feature
risk-taking allocation decisions, not enrollment/withdrawal from a savings pot
relevance_reason: Directly tests when a financial default is perceived as manipulative in a European consumer setting, the manipulation-risk question the brief asks about.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85%, but about 80% of participants initially accepted both the low default savings rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, and half still held both defaults after three years.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large firms.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a pre-set contribution level anchors most participants for years, directly warning that whichever multiplier (1x/2x/5x) is pre-selected in the round-up feature is likely to become the de facto ceiling for most users.
limitations: employer 401(k) plans, not a consumer app
no publication year given, indicating this is the classic study current literature argues with
relevance_reason: The classic result on anchoring at a pre-set contribution level, the direct precedent for the multiplier pre-selection decision.

key_finding: In 8.6 million tipping decisions, 84% of default adherence arose from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out effort cost together (friction complementarity); adding a lower option (15%) below an existing 20-25-30% menu captured 69% of achievable consumer welfare gains at only 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural model estimated on 8.6 million real transactions plus an independent stated-preference survey of preferences.
why_it_matters: The counterfactual on adding a lower preset option is a direct, quantified answer to the multiplier-menu question: it shows how much welfare is left on the table by a restrictive menu and how cheaply it can be recovered, a method that transfers straightforwardly to designing the 1x/2x/5x round-up menu.
limitations: taxi tipping, not a savings product
monetary stakes and decision frequency differ substantially from a savings sweep
relevance_reason: Named method transfer: a structural default-menu model decomposing deviation cost and opt-out cost, plus a counterfactual on adding a lower preset tier, applies directly to designing the round-up multiplier menu.

key_finding: An opt-in short-term, freely withdrawable payroll savings account had very low take-up (under 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated it), but among those who did, 96% still held a balance and 87% received an automatic contribution at 12 months.
methodology: Field study of a payroll-deduction short-term savings product introduced at five UK firms, 12-month follow-up.
why_it_matters: Closest available product analogue to a round-up pot: shows that opt-in to a liquid, withdrawable savings vehicle produces very low enrollment but strong retention among enrollees -- direct evidence for the 'quality over quantity' argument against opt-out for a liquid product.
limitations: distributed via employer payroll, retaining the trusted-intermediary mechanism the brief says does not carry over to a standalone app
no comparison to opt-out or active-choice arms
relevance_reason: The product (short-term, liquid, withdrawable savings) is structurally the closest analogue to round-up savings found in the set, despite being employer-distributed.

key_finding: A general theoretical characterization shows that when designer and choosers agree on an activity's value, weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal, with results extending to cases of designer-chooser disagreement and normative ambiguity.
methodology: Theoretical model with asymptotic analysis and numerical simulations of optimal default policy.
why_it_matters: Offers a normative lens for when opting everyone in is actually welfare-optimal versus when disagreement between what the bank wants and what users want should push toward opt-in or active choice -- useful framing for justifying whichever entry design is chosen.
limitations: pure theory with simulated validation, no empirical consumer data
no named population or product setting
relevance_reason: Provides a normative framework for judging when opt-out defaults are justified versus manipulative, relevant to the entry-design decision but not empirically grounded in the brief's setting.

key_finding: Maps EU law on dark patterns and offers a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations to distinguish acceptable choice-architecture influence from manipulation warranting regulation.
methodology: Doctrinal legal analysis and taxonomy-building; abstract-only, no empirical data.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete EU legal test for when a pre-selected opt-out default crosses from helpful nudge into a regulated dark pattern, which should directly shape whether we choose opt-out, opt-in, or active choice and how we disclose the exit.
limitations: normative/legal framework, not an empirical measure of enrolment or behavior change
not specific to financial products or round-up savings
relevance_reason: Directly addresses the brief's stated reputational risk that an opt-out default could read as a dark pattern in the EU regulatory context.

key_finding: With a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees had opted out by 12 months (versus roughly half in plans with lower defaults), and many who stayed at the default had incomes suggesting 12% was a poor fit, with low-income employees anchoring most strongly.
methodology: Administrative panel data from an employer retirement plan; longitudinal opt-out and contribution tracking to 12+ months.
why_it_matters: Shows a high preset default can anchor people at a level worse than they would otherwise choose, and that this bites hardest on lower-income savers, which bears on how aggressively we should pre-select a round-up multiplier and for whom.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a self-directed consumer app
no employer-trust intermediary in our setting
abstract gives opt-out rate but not amounts saved
relevance_reason: Directly evidences anchoring on a preset default level and heterogeneous harm to lower-income users, both named in the brief's open questions.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, automatic (passive) employer contributions raised wealth accumulation substantially while active-choice tax subsidies induced only 1 cent of new saving per dollar of subsidy, because 85% of savers are 'passive' and unresponsive to active incentives.
methodology: Large-scale administrative panel data analysis, population-level, Denmark.
why_it_matters: The canonical large-N demonstration that passive/default policies dominate active-choice-based incentives for the majority of savers, but it is the foundational retirement-plan result the brief explicitly says needs updating for a liquid, self-directed consumer app.
limitations: retirement/tax-advantaged accounts, not liquid consumer savings
government/employer intermediary mechanism does not carry to a banking app
does not address active-choice-in-onboarding as a design, only active vs passive saving behavior generally
relevance_reason: The most-cited large-scale evidence for the default effect the internal argument leans on, useful as the benchmark this project's data should be measured against but capped by domain mismatch.

key_finding: Two field experiments show 'active choice' (forcing a yes/no decision) increases desired behavior versus no intervention, and a refined 'enhanced active choice' that frames losses in the non-preferred option performs even better, recommended as a complement to or substitute for automatic enrollment.
methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments comparing active choice, enhanced active choice, and no-default conditions.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, tested alternative to full opt-out enrolment — forced active choice with loss-framed messaging — that could capture much of the enrolment lift without passively sweeping in disengaged users, directly informing the entry-mechanism decision.
limitations: field experiments are in health/medication and general savings contexts, not a mobile banking round-up feature
no 6-12 month persistence data reported in the abstract
enhanced active choice framing itself risks reading as manipulative under EU dark-pattern scrutiny
relevance_reason: The core paper testing whether active choice (and an enhanced variant) gets most of the default's benefit, which is exactly the brief's stated open question.

key_finding: Synthesizes household finance evidence including choice architecture, defaults, product design, and disclosure as levers firms and governments use to shape financial behavior, alongside empirical regularities inconsistent with classical rational-choice models.
methodology: Narrative review/book chapter synthesizing empirical household finance literature; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Provides the broad synthesis of which choice-architecture levers (defaults, product design, disclosure) actually move household financial behavior, useful as background framing for weighing the entry and level decisions together rather than in isolation.
limitations: broad overview without effect sizes specific to round-up savings or opt-out onboarding
covers many financial domains at once rather than isolating the consumer savings-app case
abstract does not specify a systematic review protocol
relevance_reason: A general review of behavioral household finance interventions that touches on several of the brief's sub-questions but at low resolution.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrolment raised participation to over 85%, but roughly 80% of participants initially accepted the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and default fund, and half still did so after three years, roughly offsetting the participation gain against a lower savings rate per person.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms tracking automatic-enrolment participants for up to three years.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that a low preset default anchors contribution levels for years, directly warning against shipping a low pre-selected round-up multiplier if the goal is meaningful savings amounts rather than nominal enrolment.
limitations: employer 401(k) plan, not a self-directed consumer app
over two decades old, predating the app/liquidity/regulatory context the brief flags as changed
does not measure withdrawal or disengagement, only contribution-rate anchoring
relevance_reason: Foundational evidence on anchoring at a preset default level, the exact mechanism the brief worries about for the round-up multiplier decision.

key_finding: Randomizing default enrolment into a salary-linked savings account increased participation by 40 percentage points, equivalent to a 50% match incentive, with the effect attributed largely to present bias and the cognitive cost of evaluating savings scenarios rather than employer trust.
methodology: Field experiment with random assignment to different default savings-account variants among salaried employees in Afghanistan, with follow-up interventions isolating mechanisms.
why_it_matters: Directly tests why defaults work (present bias, cognitive cost) rather than just that they work, which matters for predicting whether an opt-out round-up default will produce genuine engagement or just passive non-opt-out; also finds defaults increased later active saving, a data point against pure disengagement.
limitations: salary-linked account still routed through an employer paymaster, retaining some intermediary-trust mechanism the brief says doesn't transfer
developing-country labor-market setting far from an EU consumer banking app
no 6-12 month withdrawal or amount-saved data reported
relevance_reason: Offers mechanism-level evidence on why default effects occur, relevant to judging whether the same mechanism would produce engaged versus vanity enrolment in the app.
